idiom_name: useful zero value + nil-receiver methods + stdlib no-op values (io.Discard)
implementation_notes: Go absorbs the pattern into two conventions: make the zero value useful (a declared bytes.Buffer or sync.Mutex is ready to use, a nil slice and a nil map are legal to read, struct{} costs nothing) and define methods with a nil receiver when a pointer type has a meaningful absent state, so the zero value answers the interface instead of panicking. The standard library ships the same idea as values: io.Discard consumes every write, http.NoBody is an empty body and strings.NewReader("") is an empty reader. Write an explicit implementation only when the absent state must behave differently from a valid empty one; Go prefers a small interface plus a no-op implementation over a class hierarchy, and callers still commonly branch on the (value, error) pair, so the pattern is a convention here rather than a structure.
pitfalls: A nil map can be read but not written - assignment panics - so 'the zero value is useful' holds only until the first write; make or guard before storing.

A nil interface value and an interface holding a nil pointer are different: calling a method on the former panics, so the nil-receiver trick only works on concrete pointer types that test for nil themselves.

io.Discard replaces a writer, not a decision: code that must know whether anything was written still needs a real implementation, and the stdlib's own proposals rejected a magical nil *slog.Logger for exactly that reason.
Zero-value special cases invite accidental use: a Config{} that silently defaults can hide a forgotten initialisation where an error return would have been noticed.
